title: Give recordings a purposeful workflow
description: Understand workflow scope, stages and the difference between authoring a graph and operating its workers.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional logistics team. Its entrance camera and warehouse camera need different processing. Must every recording follow exactly the same choices?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Workflows let a deployment tailor routing and processing around its use case. Think about which camera matters, when the workflow should be active and which available operations should run. Start with one clear question rather than connecting every possible stage.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the workflow is the plan, while stage workers do the work?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Devices, filters and processing steps express the intent. The actual engine, queues and workers must exist to carry it out.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The guide shows a visual editor as well as deployment configuration. Which should an operator expect in an established production rollout?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The page explicitly identifies Helm-defined workflows as the current deployment path. Database-backed organisation workflows and their editor and API path are implemented capabilities, but shouldn't be presented as the established path everywhere.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Does a configuration workflow have the same reach as an organisation's stored workflow?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Configuration workflows are deployment-global; stored workflows belong to their organisation. Check scope deliberately. Naming a workflow after one location doesn't itself make a global definition private to that location.

chapters.title: Deploy and verify the whole chain

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our logistics team has a definition. What makes it ready to run?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Enable the actual workflows engine, deploy the worker for each referenced operation, and align the queues and supported result operations. The frontend feature flag only exposes workflow controls; it doesn't deploy the engine.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And how do we confirm a change is active?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Configuration changes require the documented engine rollout. Stored changes are read for subsequent recordings. Test one appropriate recording and follow its run through routing, stage dispatch and persisted output. The fixed pipeline still provides the baseline; a saved diagram is not evidence that every worker has executed.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
